articles.title: 'My parents came from India last night': Nikhil Chaudhary's emotional Player of the Match moment at MCG
articles.summary: For Nikhil Chaudhary, Saturday's memorable night at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) was about much more than scoring a match-winning 66 or picking up
articles.body: For Nikhil Chaudhary, Saturday's memorable night at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) was about much more than scoring a match-winning 66 or picking up two wickets against England. It was a special family moment as the Indian-born Australian all-rounder's parents travelled from India to watch him play for the first time, witnessing him deliver a Player of the Match performance in Australia's thrilling three-wicket victory.Born in Delhi, Chaudhary produced an outstanding all-round display in the first T20I against England, smashing 66 off just 38 deliveries before claiming two wickets for 21 runs in his four overs. His contribution helped Australia chase down England's 188-run target with one ball to spare.However, the biggest highlight for the 30-year-old came after the match when he reflected on his parents' presence at the MCG and admitted that he had never imagined receiving such an honour while representing Australia."My parents came over from India last night, so there's nothing better than getting a Man of the Match against them, and it's their first game watching me play as well," Chaudhary said after the match.'Never imagined that': Chaudhary reflects on special MCG momentAsked whether he had ever imagined becoming Player of the Match for Australia at the MCG, the all-rounder admitted that it was something he had never anticipated."No, man, never imagined that," he said, before highlighting how special it was to have his parents witness the performance.Nikhil Chaudhary stars in Australia's thrilling winChaudhary delivered an outstanding all-round performance, scoring 66 off just 38 deliveries, including five fours and two sixes. His innings proved crucial in Australia's successful chase of 188.The 30-year-old had also made an impact with the ball, claiming two wickets for just 21 runs in his four overs. He dismissed England captain Harry Brook, who top-scored with an explosive 65 off 28 deliveries, and Sam Curran, who contributed 21.Earlier, England posted 187/9 in their 20 overs after being asked to bat. Brook and Tom Banton, who scored 39, helped the visitors recover from an early setback and build a competitive total. Jordan Cox added 27, while Liam Dawson chipped in with 17. For Australia, Jack Edwards picked up two wickets, while Joel Davies, Riley Meredith, Ben Dwarshuis and Adam Zampa claimed one each.In reply, Australia got off to a shaky start after Jake Fraser-McGurk was dismissed for one, but Sam Harper (32) and captain Mitchell Marsh (37) steadied the innings.Chaudhary then took charge with his aggressive strokeplay, forming an important partnership with Tim David, who scored 20. After his dismissal for 66, Jack Edwards remained unbeaten on 25 to guide Australia home.The hosts eventually reached 191/7 in 19.5 overs, securing a three-wicket victory with one ball remaining. Chaudhary was named Player of the Match for his outstanding contribution with both bat and ball.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Big blow for Bangladesh! Star player ruled out of second Test against South Africa
articles.summary: Bangladesh have suffered a major setback ahead of the second Test against South Africa, with experienced batter Mushfiqur Rahim ruled out of the series
articles.body: Bangladesh have suffered a major setback ahead of the second Test against South Africa, with experienced batter Mushfiqur Rahim ruled out of the series finale due to a groin injury.The second Test is scheduled to begin at Centurion on November 23, with Bangladesh needing a victory to level the two-match series after going 1-0 down in Johannesburg.Mushfiqur sustained the injury during the opening Test at the Wanderers, where he complained of acute pain in his left groin. A subsequent MRI scan confirmed inflammation and irritation around the bony pelvis, forcing the team management to rule him out of the upcoming contest.Bangladesh national team physiotherapist Bayjedul Islam Khan confirmed the development, explaining that the veteran batter needs immediate rest and a rehabilitation programme to prevent the injury from worsening."Mushfiqur complained of acute pain in the left groin region during the first Test match. Following the Test, he underwent an MRI scan and the results confirmed some inflammation and irritation around the bony pelvis," Khan said."He requires immediate rest and targeted rehabilitation to manage the stress response and prevent further aggravation and is unavailable for the second Test," he added.Mushfiqur's absence comes at a difficult time for Bangladesh, who will be keen to bounce back after suffering a nine-wicket defeat in the series opener. The veteran batter had scored 22 in the first innings and 22 in the second innings of the Johannesburg Test.Meanwhile, South Africa have also been dealt an injury setback, with captain Temba Bavuma ruled out of the second Test due to a calf strain. Bavuma is expected to remain with the squad, while Aiden Markram is likely to take over the captaincy. Tony de Zorzi is tipped to come into the playing XI as his replacement.Bangladesh face uphill task to level seriesThe opening Test at the Wanderers saw Bangladesh produce a spirited fightback after an early batting collapse. From 22/3 and later 121/5, they recovered through centuries from Towhid Hridoy (137) and Litton Das (120), who put together a record 206-run partnership for the sixth wicket to take the visitors to 400.South Africa responded with a formidable 557, powered by maiden Test centuries from Marques Ackerman (157) and Ryan Rickelton (102), while Zubayr Hamza contributed 83 and Kagiso Rabada struck a career-best 72.Bangladesh fought back with the ball, but South Africa secured a sizeable 157-run first-innings advantage.In their second innings, the visitors struggled against Rabada and Simon Harmer, eventually being bowled out for 168. Harmer was the chief destroyer with figures of 6/51, while Rabada claimed three wickets.South Africa were left with a modest target of 12 runs and completed the chase to register a nine-wicket victory, taking a 1-0 lead in the series.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Make history by winning three titles in a row': RCB head coach's big statement ahead of IPL 2027
articles.summary: Defending champions Royal Challengers Bengaluru are confident of maintaining their winning combination as they prepare for the IPL 2027 auction, despite
articles.body: Defending champions Royal Challengers Bengaluru are confident of maintaining their winning combination as they prepare for the IPL 2027 auction, despite having considerably less spending power than several of their rivals.RCB, who clinched their second consecutive title by defeating Gujarat Titans by five wickets in the final in Ahmedabad this year, are targeting an unprecedented third straight IPL crown.Head coach Andy Flower said the franchise was satisfied with the core of its squad and was under no pressure to make sweeping changes at the auction, scheduled to take place in Goa on December 16.RCB have retained the bulk of their title-winning group, with Virat Kohli, Josh Hazlewood, Phil Salt and skipper Rajat Patidar among those staying on. The franchise released just five players, including injured England all-rounder Jacob Bethell, leaving them with Rs 14.15 crore to fill five available slots, one of which is reserved for an overseas player."We have had two very strong years, and going into the third year of this cycle, we are very confident and comfortable with the squad we have," Flower said on JioStar's 'TATA IPL 2027 Retention Special'.While acknowledging the need to use the auction to improve the squad, Flower admitted that RCB would have limited financial flexibility compared to other franchises."We have made a few releases and the responsibility at an auction is always to improve your squad, and we will be looking to do that."But we will be more limited than some of the other sides in the auction when it comes to spending power."We are comfortable with that because we have retained the bulk of our squad and a very strong core, the players who have served us so well over the last couple of years. We will be looking for that combination to work well again for us in 2027, and we have a very important season ahead where we can make history by winning three titles in a row."GT explain decision to release IshantMeanwhile, Gujarat Titans assistant coach Parthiv Patel acknowledged that parting ways with experienced India pacer Ishant Sharma was a difficult call, given the influence he had within the dressing room.Ishant, who spent the last two seasons with the franchise, did not feature in a single match last season. GT also released Luke Wood and Connor Esterhuizen as they looked to make changes to their squad."It is not the easiest of decisions to let go of players, but Ishant Sharma has been with us for the last two seasons, and he was such a great influence on the players."For a player who has played 100 Test matches for India to then not get a game in an IPL season is something that is difficult. The same goes for Luke Wood and Connor Esterhuizen. That is the main reason why we have let go of certain players."We also have to see that in this three-year cycle since the last mega auction, we have had a good bit of success. We qualified for the playoffs in 2025, we played in the final last season, so there was not much need to let go of a high number of players. We are quite happy with the way things are at the moment as far as our team combination is concerned, so we have not let go of many players," he said.GT have brought in Harshal Patel from Sunrisers Hyderabad through a trade, with Parthiv identifying the experienced pacer as the answer to the void left by Ishant.The Gujarat-born bowler's familiarity with local conditions, coupled with his death-over expertise, made him an important addition to the squad, Parthiv said."Harshal Patel's inclusion is an important addition for us. We have let go of the experience of Ishant Sharma, so we needed someone with that kind of experience in our squad. Harshal is also a player who is from Gujarat. He understands these conditions really well. On top of everything, he brings a lot of quality. He brings that death-bowling specialist role, which we were always looking for," he said.Highlighting Harshal's consistency and ability to handle pressure, Parthiv added that his variations would give the team another reliable option in the closing stages of an innings."His record in the IPL speaks for itself. He has been one of the most consistent wicket-takers in the death overs, and he knows how to bowl on flat wickets and in pressure situations. He also brings that experience of playing big matches, which helps the younger bowlers in the squad."With his variations and his ability to bowl the yorker and the slower ball, he gives us a strong option at the back end of the innings. That is exactly what we needed after losing an experienced campaigner like Ishant. When you have a local player like that and the opportunity comes up, that is the reason why we traded for Harshal to bring him into our team," he added.KKR look to add batting firepowerKolkata Knight Riders, meanwhile, have identified their batting department as the primary area requiring attention ahead of the auction.Head coach Abhishek Nayar said the franchise had explored the trade market but would now look to use the auction to bring in the firepower needed to strengthen the batting line-up."Batting is a department we want to strengthen. You try your hand at trades and hope that it works, but sometimes when it does not, you want to go into the auction and get the kind of firepower that can strengthen your batting," Nayar said.Nayar was satisfied with KKR's bowling performances, pointing out that the team had topped the rankings for wickets taken and performed consistently across different phases of the game."With regard to bowling, I felt we did really well. We were the number-one-ranked team when it came to picking up wickets and doing well in different phases of the game. But batting is an aspect we definitely want to strengthen."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Bigger than Hansie Cronje's match-fixing': Legendary cricketer makes explosive Sandpaper Gate claim
articles.summary: England great Geoffrey Boycott has launched a fresh attack on former Australia captain Steven Smith over his involvement in the infamous 2018 Sandpaper
articles.body: England great Geoffrey Boycott has launched a fresh attack on former Australia captain Steven Smith over his involvement in the infamous 2018 Sandpaper Gate scandal, insisting that history should judge him harshly for failing to prevent the ball-tampering plot.Boycott believes Smith cannot escape responsibility by claiming he chose not to involve himself in the plan after it was discussed by his teammates. The former Australian skipper was present when David Warner suggested using abrasive material to generate reverse swing and Cameron Bancroft agreed to carry out the act. However, rather than intervening, Smith told the team that he did not want to know anything further about it.In his column for The Telegraph, Boycott argued that Smith had failed in his primary duty as captain by allowing the plan to proceed.“As captain, Smith should have put a stop to it as soon as Warner raised the idea of using sandpaper," Boycott wrote.“For him to say ‘I don’t want to know about it’, yet let it go ahead and accept the unfair benefits of cheating and think that somehow it absolved him as not being part of it is staggering. History should not be kind to Smith. He abrogated his responsibility as a captain."Smith had accepted responsibility for his involvement and served a one-year ban imposed by Cricket Australia. According to Usman Khawaja, who revisited the controversy in his book Sabr, Smith took the punishment in an attempt to shield his teammates.'Bigger than Hansie Cronje's match-fixing'Boycott also offered a strong assessment of the scale of the scandal, claiming it was even more damaging than the match-fixing controversy involving former South Africa captain Hansie Cronje in 2000.While there has been debate over whether Cricket Australia's punishment was excessive, given that ball-tampering has long been a part of cricket and is covered under ICC regulations, Boycott believes the Sandpaper Gate episode was unprecedented.Cronje was stripped of the South African captaincy and eventually received a lifetime ban after admitting to accepting money from bookmakers to influence matches.However, Boycott argued that the Australian scandal was more extensive because it involved an entire team rather than a handful of individuals.“The sandpaper scandal is even bigger than Hansie Cronje’s match-fixing, which ripped apart South Africa cricket more than 25 years ago. This is bigger than anything I have read or seen in cricket: a whole team cheating. Cronje’s crimes mainly involved him recruiting a couple of junior players… but sandpaper involved the whole Australian team. The squad and coaches were all up to their necks in it, plotting and planning to cheat en masse, and the cover-up let three players take the blame," he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'As Mumbai Indians we feel like underdogs now. We need to earn our straps back': Batting coach Robin Uthappa
articles.summary: Dubai: Robin Uthappa's appointment as Mumbai Indians' (MI) batting coach comes at a time when the five-time Indian Premier League (IPL) champions are
articles.body: Dubai: Robin Uthappa's appointment as Mumbai Indians' (MI) batting coach comes at a time when the five-time Indian Premier League (IPL) champions are looking to reset after a disappointing campaign and a period of transition within their coaching set-up. Uthappa, who has spent the last few years working with batters behind the scenes, steps into the franchise environment for the first time as a coach, bringing with him years of IPL experience as a player and a fresh perspective on batting.His IPL journey took him to six teams, ranging from MI, Royal Challengers Bengaluru (RCB), Pune Warriors India (PWI), Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR), Rajasthan Royals (RR) and Chennai Super Kings (CSK). He played 205 matches, scoring 4952 runs at a strike of 130.35, including 27 fifties.Currently in Dubai as a commentator for the ILT20, Uthappa spoke about his appointment, his coaching philosophy, the importance of building trust with players and the challenge of helping MI rediscover their winning culture.Excerpts:Q. Robin, you were known as a cricketer and commentator. When did you become a coach?Uthappa: When did I become a coach? As of 2 months ago, officially for a franchise... for MI. I have always been coaching. After I finished playing... I do personal coaching. Predominantly focused on batting. It is something that I have been doing for the last three to four years now. In Dubai. I do more one-on-one coaching. I don't do group coaching. I like to focus on individual cricketers and help them improve their game.I continue to work with international and domestic cricketers in India as well. I do it very under the radar. Very low profile. They have consistently been doing well over the last two to three years in domestic and international cricket as well. I would rather them speak about it than me speak about it. The intention is not to build a profile out of it, but to genuinely add value. That was always my intention of working with them.As Mumbai Indians, we feel like we are underdogs. We really need to earn our straps back and earn the trust of the fansQ. How did the MI association happen?Uthappa: It was just completely leftfield. Completely came from the leftfield. I didn't see it coming. The interest was there. I have been hoping that I got a call at some point to work with a franchise. I felt that I could add a lot of value. When the call came from the management, the interest was there from my side. The conversations happened and the interest was there.Q. What can we expect from you? What are your plans for MI?Uthappa: As a batting coach, you first want to add value to the group, create a good atmosphere and culture within the group. To make sure that everyone feels happy. A happy environment is a thriving environment. As in life, you can't guarantee success in sport. We only have to make sure we give the athletes the best chance to be successful. (So you) help create the atmosphere that makes people really enjoy what they are doing. The intent is to go out there and build that culture and environment. To make sure there is a happy ecosystem. As Mumbai Indians, we feel like we are underdogs. We really need to earn our straps back and earn the trust of the fans. A lot of things (that) we have to work towards as a group.Q. Working with people like Rohit Sharma, Suryakumar Yadav, Tilak Varma. What do you think about it? How do you look forward to it?Uthappa: As established cricketers, having clarity is important. Nobody is bigger than mother cricket. We have all been in the game long enough to know that nobody can beat mother cricket. Nobody can supersede mother cricket. You have to operate from that humility. You give yourself the best chance to do well when you navigate through the game as a student of the game, rather than the master.You can be as established as you want. As athletes, you always want to have clarity before a tournament begins. You want to have clarity around your own game, the team's motives and team's goals. Aligning those two aspects is also important. There are a lot of aspects that established players also require.As a coach, we can serve them by making sure that as far as preparation is concerned, we give them everything they need to feel like they are ready to perform. They feel happy and confident about where they are before a match begins. There are so many things that a coach can do.You can just be there and be available for them to even have a conversation. Sometimes just being available is such a big blessing for established players. There is an umpteen number of things that can be done. It is exciting and challenging.You give yourself the best chance to do well when you navigate through the game as a student of the game, rather than the master.When you look at athletes, the legacy comes after the career is over. While they are playing cricket, they are still playing the game. They are still humble about playing the sport. They don't think of themselves as World Cup champions. They don't think of themselves as a captain who has won this five times. It adds a lot of value when you talk about it from a team perspective.But you will not find cricketers individually thinking, I am a World Cup-winning captain, I don't need to hear anything. Everyone is really humble and they understand the deeper nuances of the game.Q. For the MI, it is an entirely new start and obviously there is going to be a new captain as well. But has there been initial conversations between the new group, especially with the auction coming up?Uthappa: Now that the auction is actually coming up, there are obviously things that you don't want to talk about at this point. There are a lot of moving pieces and you have to navigate through all of those quite carefully. So, probably a good time to chat would be post the auction about these things.Q. In T20s, there are people like Vaibhav Sooryavanshi at Rajasthan Royals, Abhishek Sharma at Sunrisers Hyderabad. MI doesn't seem to have anyone of that calibre. There are good stroke players but not somebody with 250-plus strike rate at the top of the line. How do you address that challenge?Uthappa: Well, I think it depends on having the conversations with the existing players and there is an auction coming up. So, to see what possibilities are there in perhaps picking one of them up.But honestly, if you ask me, I think the talent is there in the existing side itself. There is enough and more talent to prove that they are worth their weight in gold. And these personnel are enough to perform exceptionally well.I think it's almost uncanny what you can actually draw out of players when you create the right atmosphere for them to go out there and play good cricket.Q. Robin, what is the brand of coaching that you bring to the table and do you want to also implement wherever you go?Uthappa: Well, I think the brand of coaching that I would exercise and I have always exercised is one where I try to meet players where they are and help them elevate themselves to where they want to be.It has to be driven by the athlete themselves. I am only but a mirror to them to hold them accountable for the things that they want to achieve for themselves and align that to the larger goal of the team. And I think any good coach's job is to make sure that any athlete is as well prepared as they possibly can be and feel ready for competition.I think those are more larger aspects but I think the more finer ones are the ones where you earn the trust of a player for them to feel like I can just pick up the phone or I can go to him and I can actually have a conversation with him about my career because those are the most important aspects about an athlete's life and those are not aspects that they are willing to open up to anybody else. So I think earning the trust of a player is extremely crucial for me as a coach and that is something that I put for myself of highest value.Q. In this day and age, there is very little time to actually implement any sort of technical changes. You go from one game to another and there is very little turnaround time. Does that make your job even tougher?Uthappa: It is, I wouldn't say a challenge, but I would say it can be hard because when you see a deficiency in a player or you see a biomechanical fix that's available to make more than a technical fix. When we talk about technical fixes, it's basically biomechanical fixes.It's the biomechanics that you want to alter or adjust a little bit that helps about achieve what the player wants to feel while they are batting. So when you are talking about those aspects, I have gone through two batting transformations in my own personal career and I've been through the ringer to actually achieve that. So for me, my learnings from all of that has been I have figured out a way to help athletes or help batters make adjustments in their biomechanics to find the shortest way, or the path, to where they want to be and about feeling good about their own batting. And this is something that I have done for a few years right now. It's something that I did even as a senior pro while I was playing cricket professionally. So for me, that is something that I think I've done my rite of passage.So people have seen me go through that. A lot of the existing players have also seen me go through those batting transformations. So I think they understand the value of what it actually takes to go through breaking yourself down to your foundations and building yourself up again ... because I've done that, I've figured out mediums of adjusting biomechanics to serve a batter.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Fighter jet gestures: Umpire celebrates with Pakistan team after controversial Asia Cup win; India questions neutrality
articles.summary: The Cricket Association for the Blind in India (CABI) has questioned the neutrality of a Pakistani umpire after a video appeared to show him celebrating
articles.body: The Cricket Association for the Blind in India (CABI) has questioned the neutrality of a Pakistani umpire after a video appeared to show him celebrating with Pakistan players through gestures that seemed to mimic aircrafts crashing. The incident has added to the tensions between the two teams following the controversy over the rain-hit Men's Asia Cup for the Blind final in Dhaka.India's blind cricket team had boycotted the trophy presentation ceremony after Pakistan were declared champions despite the final being washed out without a ball being bowled. CABI has now raised concerns over the umpire's conduct, saying match officials must remain neutral and should not be seen celebrating with either team.“This Pakistani umpire officiated throughout the Asia Cup Cricket for the Blind 2026, yet is seen celebrating with the Pakistan team,” CABI said in a statement.“As per the principles of officiating, an umpire must remain neutral and should never be seen aligning with any team,” the association added.The latest row follows Pakistan being awarded the title on the basis of a superior run rate after rain prevented the final from taking place. India had argued that both teams should have been declared joint winners, as there was no reserve day, instead of deciding the title through net run rate.The controversy grew after World Blind Cricket Council (WBCC) president and Pakistan Blind Cricket Council chief Sultan Shah reportedly overruled the WBCC Technical Committee's recommendation to declare India and Pakistan joint winners. The match referee was then directed to announce Pakistan as champions.CABI general secretary Shailendra Yadav accused Pakistan of unilaterally declaring themselves champions, alleging that the decision disregarded the position of the World Blind Cricket Council (WBCC) Technical Committee."I am deeply disappointed and strongly condemn the manner in which Pakistan has declared itself the winner of the Blind Cricket Asia Cup final without a single ball being bowled," Yadav said in a statement.In protest, the Indian players stayed away from the trophy presentation ceremony.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: IND vs NZ 1st Test: Bossing the Basin! KL Rahul's 13th Test ton, Shubman Gill's 98 put India in command
articles.summary: KL Rahul once again proved his technical proficiency in overseas conditions and marked his maiden Test appearance in New Zealand with a typically measured
articles.body: KL Rahul once again proved his technical proficiency in overseas conditions and marked his maiden Test appearance in New Zealand with a typically measured hundred, before skipper Shubman Gill raised the tempo with a counterattacking and stylish 98 as India tightened their grip on the opening Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Saturday.By stumps on Day 3, India, resuming at 159-1, had surged to 486-4 — a lead of 118 — with Rishabh Pant unbeaten on 55. It was an extraordinary collective batting effort, with each of India’s top five crossing fifty in an overseas Test innings for the first time.If Rahul’s 136 off 296 balls, with nine fours and two sixes, laid the foundation, Gill’s 98 off 146 balls, with nine fours and two sixes, provided the impetus. India needed that as they looked to build a lead big enough to avoid batting again and give their bowlers sufficient time to force a result on a placid pitch.Rahul and Devdutt Padikkal (80 off 175; 10x4) carried the momentum from India’s batting effort on Day 2, although the Kiwi bowlers put in an impressive pre-lunch effort. Matt Henry and Nathan Smith operated with ’keeper Tom Blundell standing up to the stumps as Rahul and Padikkal embraced denial and banished extravagance.It meant India’s first run of the morning came only off the 21st delivery and five of the first six overs were maidens. Padikkal completed a composed half-century and Rahul gradually began to open up, even dancing down the track to loft Glenn Phillips over long-on with a shot that almost struck a baby in the stands — much to Rahul’s anguish.Rahul and Padikkal went through the entire first session without being separated, adding 80 in 27 overs.Soon after lunch, Rahul nudged Jacob Duffy for a single to complete his 13th Test century. The India vice-captain became only the fourth Indian, after Sachin Tendulkar, Mohammed Azharuddin and Rahul Dravid, to score Test hundreds in all four SENA countries — South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia — and the first Indian opener to accomplish the feat.The second-wicket partnership had reached 165 when Kyle Jamieson finally produced something special with the second new ball. Bowling from around the wicket, he got one to hold its line and hit the top of Padikkal’s off stump.Gill arrived with intent. Sensing that Rahul had started tiring, the captain looked to push the scoring rate. Rahul eventually dragged a Smith delivery onto his stumps for 136 after adding 91 with Gill.If the hosts thought getting Rahul would provide some respite, they were mistaken. In Rishabh Pant, India had the ideal batter to take advantage of a flagging attack. Initially content to turn the strike over to Gill, Pant exploded once he found his range.In between sporadic coughs and witty barbs, he hooked Duffy for two sixes and a four in one over and raced to his 22nd Test half-century off 55 balls.Gill, meanwhile, continued to attack, using his feet beautifully against spin. India crossed 400 and then pushed their lead beyond 100.The day, however, ended with personal disappointment for Gill. Having spent more than eight overs in the 90s, an overanxious Gill fell two short of his century when Duffy adjusted the square-leg and deep fine-leg fielders to give him the impression that a short ball was coming. Instead, Duffy bowled a full delivery that seamed back in and breached the skipper’s defence.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: Rishabh Pant added another special achievement to his name on Sunday, becoming the first Indian wicketkeeper to score Test centuries in all four SENA
articles.body: Rishabh Pant added another special achievement to his name on Sunday, becoming the first Indian wicketkeeper to score Test centuries in all four SENA countries - South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia.The left-handed batter reached the milestone with an attacking century on Day 4 of the first Test against New Zealand at the Basin Reserve in Wellington.Pant, 29, was playing his first match for India since the tour of Sri Lanka in August. He brought up his hundred in just 135 balls. At 99, he played a cheeky reverse-sweep off part-time spinner Glenn Phillips, sending the ball past short third man. On the very next delivery, he stepped down the track and hit Phillips over mid-off for a six to complete his century.Pant was eventually caught at deep midwicket for 128 off 153 balls. However, his knock had helped India take a 261-run lead by the lunch break.Joins an elite listPant became only the sixth Indian batter to score Test centuries in all four SENA countries. The other five are Mohammad Azharuddin, Sachin Tendulkar, Rahul Dravid, Virat Kohli and KL Rahul.Rahul entered the list a day earlier, becoming the first Indian opener to achieve the feat.Asian batters with Test centuries in all four SENA countries:Mohammad AzharuddinSachin TendulkarSaeed AnwarRahul DravidYounis KhanKumar SangakkaraVirat KohliKL RahulRishabh PantPakistan's Saeed Anwar and Younis Khan, along with Sri Lanka's Kumar Sangakkara, are the other Asian batters to have achieved this feat.Among wicketkeepers from around the world, only Australia's Adam Gilchrist and England's Jonny Bairstow have also scored Test hundreds in all four SENA countries.Third on the list of most Test hundreds by wicketkeepersThe Wellington century was Pant's ninth in Test cricket as a designated wicketkeeper. That remains his highest Test score.In January 2022, he scored an unbeaten 100 in Cape Town against South Africa. Later that year, he hit 146 against England at Edgbaston.Last year, Pant continued his good run in England, scoring 134 and 118 at Leeds.Pant shows no signs of rust after injury breakPant's return to international cricket was closely watched after he missed India's entire four-day series against New Zealand A due to a left-side strain.Before that, he had led Rest of India in the Irani Cup match against Ranji Trophy champions Jammu & Kashmir in Srinagar in October.However, he looked in excellent touch in Wellington and showed no signs of being short of match practice.Pant scored most of his runs on the leg side, using his trademark slog sweeps and powerful shots. He also used his feet well to hit the ball over the bowler's head.Moves past McCullum in Test sixes listPant's attacking century also helped him move past former New Zealand captain Brendon McCullum in the list of most sixes in Test cricket.He now has 108 sixes, putting him second on the list behind England captain Ben Stokes, who has 138.Most sixes in Test cricket138 – Ben Stokes (Balls per six: 90.05)108 – Rishabh Pant (Balls per six: 47.93)107 – Brendon McCullum (Balls per six: 93.39)100 – Adam Gilchrist (Balls per six: 67.92)98 – Jacques Kallis (Balls per six: 294.87)98 – Chris Gayle (Balls per six: 122.11)98 – Tim Southee (Balls per six: 27.70)Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India delivered a remarkable batting performance against New Zealand in the first Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Sunday.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India delivered a remarkable batting performance against New Zealand in the first Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Sunday. The visitors declared their innings at 720/9 on Day 4, building a massive 352-run lead.In the process, India registered the highest-ever team total in a Test innings in New Zealand. They broke the previous record of 715/6 declared, which the hosts had scored against Bangladesh in Hamilton in 2019.KL Rahul and Rishabh Pant were the stars with the bat, scoring 136 and 128 respectively. Glenn Phillips was the most successful New Zealand bowler, finishing with figures of 3/154.India declared their innings around an hour before tea, with Dhruv Jurel being the last batter to get out. New Zealand had scored 368 in their first innings, leaving them with a huge challenge after India's batting effort.India set new record for highest Test total in New ZealandIndia's 720/9 became the biggest total ever scored in a Test innings on New Zealand soil. The previous best was the hosts' 715/6 declared against Bangladesh in Hamilton in 2019.India also broke the record for the highest Test total against New Zealand. The West Indies had earlier held the record with their 660/5 declared at the Basin Reserve in Wellington in 1995.India's highest Test totals against New Zealand720/9 declared – Wellington, 2026 (Won)583/7 declared – Ahmedabad, 1999 (Draw)566/8 declared – Nagpur, 2010 (Won)557/5 declared – Indore, 2016 (Won)537/3 declared – Chennai, 1956 (Won)India had crossed 500 runs in a Test innings in New Zealand only once before this match. They scored 520 all out against the hosts in Hamilton in 2009.Six consecutive 50-plus partnershipsIndia's innings also featured a rare batting record. Each of their first six partnerships added at least 50 runs.This has happened only four times in Test cricket. Australia first achieved it against West Indies in Brisbane in 1960-61. Pakistan followed with a similar effort against Bangladesh in Khulna in 2015.India also managed the feat against Australia in Ahmedabad in 2023. Their performance in Wellington makes them the first team to achieve it twice.Another unusual record came from India's top five batters, with each of them scoring at least 80 runs. articles.title: Rishabh Pant: Of an endless trial and unreal consistency - the MVP checks in!
articles.summary: Wellington: The last 12 months have been a wild ride for Rishabh Pant in international cricket.
articles.body: Wellington: The last 12 months have been a wild ride for Rishabh Pant in international cricket. From losing his Test vice-captaincy to getting axed from the ODI squad, the wicketkeeper-batter experienced one of the lowest phases of his career. Just like his bottom hand coming off the bat while going big, Pant was losing his grip on his cricket. It's never easy for any cricketer to maintain Pant-like standards in the toughest format, and here was Pant, hoping to do something only he could conceive.Turbulence has largely remained the undertone whenever he has stepped onto the cricket field. Even off the field, the chatter and noise continue to put him on a constant trial, where his indecision at the MCG and Guwahati overshadows eight-plus years of consistency.Usual drama preceded his arrival in New Zealand for the Test series preparations. An injury during the Irani Cup meant he wasn't supposed to get ideal game time, like most of his teammates. However, he landed, shook off the jet lag and was back doing Pant things, this time even better.Even without intention, Pant ends up playing for the gallery. It's a wild ride best enjoyed with a box full of hot chips, and he didn't disappoint the spectators soaking in the sun on the grass banks. Initially, during his 100-run partnership with Shubman Gill, Pant was losing balance, struggling for shape and didn't quite middle the ball as well as he would have liked.Then came the loud shout from the middle, where he asked for a bat change, and Mohammed Siraj knew exactly which piece of willow to fetch from the kit bag. The move worked as he hit Jacob Duffy for back-to-back sixes, found a boundary and struck the "Pantastic" note he was struggling to find. Captain Gill became a mere spectator when the fireworks were underway from the other end.The half-century was up, and the waltz from 15 to 50 runs received a loud roar from the spectators. The left-hander scored just 15 off the first 37 deliveries he faced but scored his next 37 runs in just 18 deliveries. Gill, meanwhile, could only move from 91 to 98. The initial measured start soon transformed into fluency, and Pant now held the key to India's strength and their grip on the contest.The morning of Day 4 was going to be crucial, and the roles reversed briefly when Anshul Kamboj took over the scoring intensity from Pant. But when he got back on strike and got his eye in, boundaries began to flow from both ends, and the left-hander was into the 90s. It seemed like a matter of two shots, but Pant wasn't going to throw it away in search of the glory shot. It seemed he badly wanted the magic number, even if it meant waiting 15 deliveries before creating history.At 99, there was palpable tension in the stands because there was a strong anticipation of something wild waiting to happen. A few phones were out, and Pant got the glory hit, ensuring a strong connection to clear the ropes. Out came the helmet, followed by a look to the heavens. There were no wild punches or somersaults, just a gentle raise of the bat, soaking in the applause and feeling relieved after silencing critics, again.Pant became the only wicketkeeper-batter in the world to complete the SENA set when he reached his ninth Test hundred, and four of them were scored in typical Pant fashion, with a six. He got out looking to go big again, and the naysayers will be out with their swords again, questioning the timing of the hit close to Lunch.But Pant, being Pant, will shrug off the noise, take fresh guard and again dance down the track, losing grip of the bottom hand while looking to clear the ropes.Like him or hate him, you can't ignore him.That's Rishabh Pant for you.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Two innings, two first-over strikes! Jasprit Bumrah becomes only third Indian bowler in Test history to achieve rare feat
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Jasprit Bumrah struck in the first over of New Zealand's second innings to dismiss captain Tom Latham on Day 4 of the opening Test at the Basin
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Jasprit Bumrah struck in the first over of New Zealand's second innings to dismiss captain Tom Latham on Day 4 of the opening Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Sunday.It was the second time in the match that Bumrah had picked up a wicket in his opening over. The India pacer had also dismissed Latham in the first innings, bowling him when the New Zealand skipper decided to leave the delivery.Latham survived the first ball of Bumrah's second spell, which swung into him. However, the next delivery ended his stay at the crease. Bumrah bowled a slightly shorter and wider delivery that moved away after pitching. Latham went for the shot but got an edge, which wicketkeeper Rishabh Pant safely collected.With this dismissal, Bumrah joined an elite group of Indian bowlers who have taken a wicket in the first over of both innings of a Test match.Bumrah joins Sreesanth, Zaheer KhanBumrah became only the third Indian bowler to achieve the feat, joining S Sreesanth and Zaheer Khan.Indian bowlers to take a wicket in the first over of both innings of a TestS Sreesanth vs West Indies, Kingston, 2006Zaheer Khan vs Bangladesh, Mirpur, 2007Jasprit Bumrah vs New Zealand, Wellington, 2026Where data is availableThe dismissal also added an unwanted record to Latham's name. He became only the third New Zealand captain to score a pair in a Test match. A pair is when a batter gets out for zero in both innings.Harry Cave achieved the feat in 1956, while Stephen Fleming did so in 1997.Henry Nicholls, who scored an unbeaten 175 in the first innings, opened his account in the second innings with a boundary, edging Bumrah past gully for four.India declare at 720/9, take massive 352-run leadEarlier, India declared their first innings at 720/9 in 166 overs to take a massive 352-run lead over New Zealand.It was the highest total by a team in a Test innings in New Zealand. Several Indian batters made significant contributions to the record-breaking effort.KL Rahul led the scoring with 136, while Rishabh Pant made 128. Shubman Gill scored 90, Yashasvi Jaiswal contributed 85, Devdutt Padikkal made 80 and Dhruv Jurel added 78.Jurel leads late charge before India declareDhruv Jurel and Washington Sundar continued India's charge at the start of the afternoon session. The pair added more than 50 runs without much trouble, helping India extend their lead.With Kyle Jamieson off the field, their partnership meant that all seven of India's first batting partnerships had crossed the 50-run mark. It was the first time such a feat had been achieved in Test cricket.Jurel brought up his half-century in 61 balls, playing with patience and avoiding unnecessary risks. However, Ravindra broke the partnership by dismissing Washington, who scored 24 off 26 balls.Akash Deep provided some late entertainment with two sixes in a quick five-ball 13 before Glenn Phillips dismissed him in the deep.Jurel then hit a shot towards long-on off Phillips, but Daryl Mitchell failed to hold on to the catch as the ball went for four. Jurel followed it up with a six but was stumped off the next delivery. India then declared at 720/9.India's third-highest Test totalIndia's 720/9 surpassed New Zealand's previous record of 715/6 declared against Bangladesh in Hamilton in 2019. It was also India's highest Test total away from home and their third-highest score overall.India's highest Test totals remain 759/7 declared against England in Chennai in 2016 and 726/9 declared against Sri Lanka at the Brabourne Stadium in 2009.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Before Gilchrist and Sangakkara, there was Les Ames: England great with 102  centuries whose record Rishabh Pant broke in Wellington
articles.summary: Box-office Rishabh Pant was at his brutal best against New Zealand in the first Test in Wellington, scoring 128 off 153 balls to register his ninth Test
articles.body: Box-office Rishabh Pant was at his brutal best against New Zealand in the first Test in Wellington, scoring 128 off 153 balls to register his ninth Test century.With this hundred, Pant became the sixth Indian batter to score a Test century in all four SENA countries, joining Mohammad Azharuddin, Sachin Tendulkar, Rahul Dravid, Virat Kohli and KL Rahul.Pant also climbed to second place on the list of most sixes in Test cricket, going past former New Zealand batter Brendon McCullum. He hit six sixes during his knock to take his tally to 108, one more than McCullum's 107. England's Ben Stokes leads the list with 138 sixes.The century also took Pant to third place on the list of most Test hundreds by a designated wicketkeeper. He moved past former England wicketkeeper Les Ames, who had scored eight centuries in 47 Tests. Pant now has nine hundreds, with only Adam Gilchrist (17) and Andy Flower (12) ahead of him.Most Test hundreds as a designated wicketkeeper17 - Adam Gilchrist12 - Andy Flower9 - Rishabh Pant8 - Les AmesWho was Les Ames?Leslie Ethelbert George Ames died suddenly at his home in Canterbury on February 26, 1990, aged 84.Ames passed away before Adam Gilchrist, Andy Flower and Kumar Sangakkara made their mark in the game. In his obituary, Wisden described him as someone who “was without a doubt the greatest wicketkeeper-batsman the game has so far produced.”Ames averaged more than 40 in Test cricket and scored eight centuries in 47 matches. He was considered the best batter among regular wicketkeepers of his time, ahead of players such as Jeff Dujon.When fully fit, Ames was England's first-choice wicketkeeper from 1931 to 1939, when he virtually gave up the role.He scored 2,434 runs in 47 Tests for England and was involved in 97 dismissals, including 74 catches and 23 stumpings. Ames toured Australia with M.C.C. in 1928-29 as reserve wicketkeeper to Duckworth. He was expected to play in the final Test at Melbourne as a specialist batter, but a broken finger while keeping to Larwood ruled him out. He made his Test debut against South Africa at The Oval in 1929. His final Test appearance came against South Africa in Durban in 1939.An efficient wicketkeeperAmes was popular with spectators across the country, but praise and attention did not affect him. He remained focused on his game and maintained a consistent standard behind the stumps.Among his notable performances for England were eight dismissals against West Indies at The Oval in 1933. During the 1938-39 series against South Africa, he conceded only one bye for every 275 balls delivered. On the Bodyline tour, he handled the fast bowling of Harold Larwood and Bill Voce with quiet efficiency.His wicketkeeping style was simple, with no flamboyant gestures. His glovework was neat and economical, while his stumpings were described as almost apologetic.A true man of KentAmes was a key member of Kent's Championship side from 1927 until the first match of the 1951 season. His career came to an end when a recurrence of a long-standing back problem forced him to stop playing while he was at the crease.By then, he had scored 37,248 runs in first-class cricket at an average of 43.51, including 102 centuries and nine double-centuries. He crossed 1,000 runs in a season 17 times, reached 3,000 runs once and scored 2,000 runs in five seasons.Ames was directly involved in 1,121 dismissals, with more than 1,000 of them coming when he was keeping wicket.After retiring, he continued to be associated with cricket as an administrator, manager and selector.When Ames died in February 1990, Wisden paid tribute to him in his obituary, writing: “If ever there was a true man of Kent, it was he.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: India vs New Zealand: Eight wickets or 90 overs? Who blinks first in Wellington
articles.summary: WELLINGTON: India will need eight wickets on a lifeless pitch to register a historic Test win at the Basin Reserve.
articles.body: WELLINGTON: India will need eight wickets on a lifeless pitch to register a historic Test win at the Basin Reserve. The visitors have enjoyed a strong grip on the match and are just one push away from taking a 1-0 lead in the two-match series.However, the pitch offers little hope, but the visitors are still better placed than the hosts, who must bat for a long time to secure a draw, the only favourable outcome possible at this stage. At stumps on Day 4, New Zealand were 119 for 2, trailing by 233 runs.They are two down, having lost the wickets of Tom Latham and Henry Nicholls, and will need to bat out of their skins to frustrate Jasprit Bumrah & Co. Both Devon Conway and Rachin Ravindra have been very solid since coming together in the 23rd over but must continue doing so for a long time.Signs of what to expect on Day 5 were quite evident in India's fielding placements and plans. Factoring in the slowness and lowness of the surface, there were more catchers in front of the wicket than behind it. Even Nicholls fell to that trap, thanks to a brilliant catch by Dhruv Jurel, and all the fast bowlers were very consistent in keeping the stumps in play.It was going to be their best chance to keep the hosts in check, as surviving the odd shooter will be a real challenge for the opposition. India have enough variety in the attack, and if the forecast for strong winds comes true, conditions will be toughest on the final day. India would have liked at least two more wickets before the umpires flipped the bails, especially after Latham bagged a pair when Bumrah got rid of him with the second ball.Since nothing was happening off the surface, it was going to be a patient game, with the hope that a batter would err in his decision-making. Both Nicholls and Devon Conway avoided errors until a piece of brilliance from Dhruv Jurel gave Prasidh Krishna his second wicket of the Test. The dangerman Nicholls was back in the hut, and unlike in the first innings, Prasidh wasn't the short-ball enforcer, as he stuck to the stumps line.Even Washington Sundar had a containing role to play and could well move to an attacking one if the pitch deteriorates further on the final day. There was no visible bite for the off-spinner yet, but Day 5 can throw up notorious tricks. If the wind picks up, even drift comes into play, making Sundar far more effective.All Indian bowlers have bowled many overs, and the captain needs to monitor their workload since the turnaround time between the two Tests is short. Shorter and stronger spells are going to be the order of the day, with the onus on Bumrah to lead the inexperienced pack. India have been in similar positions in different parts of the world during the ongoing World Test Championship cycle. While the result didn't go their way in Leeds and Colombo, they would hope to return with better memories from Wellington.Brief ScoresNew Zealand: 368 & 119/2 after 45 overs (Devon Conway 59 batting; Prasidh Krishna 1/20, Jasprit Bumrah 1/33)India: 720/9 declared (KL Rahul 136, Rishabh Pant 128, Shubman Gill 98, Yashasvi Jaiswal 85, Dhruv Jurel 78; Glenn Phillips 3/154, Rachin Ravindra 2/44)Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: What Sandpapergate reveals about Australian cricket
articles.summary: A toxic culture of winning at any cost has been hiding behind the myth of ‘mateship’.
articles.body:
“I knew it was wrong. I knew that using sandpaper was not simply pushing the boundaries of the laws of cricket. It was cheating,” former Australian Test cricketer Cameron Bancroft wrote in a 4,000-word expose.

His frank admission that he knowingly cheated and then lied to investigators and the Australian public was raw.

The footage of Bancroft shoving sandpaper down the front of his trousers, in an attempt to hide his illegal ball tampering during the 2018 Test series between South Africa and Australia, has been seen all over the world; the act of cheating has never been in question.

But the fallout, eight years in the making, no longer centres on a square of sandpaper. It revolves around a culture that placed winning above sound ethics. It created such deep-seated fear that lying – both directly and by omission – became a means to survive, and ultimately exposed the national belief that Australian men’s cricket was underpinned by a sacred sense of “mateship” – standing above self-interest – as a myth.

The basic facts of Australia’s ball-tampering scandal have long been established. Bancroft, with the tacit encouragement of teammate David Warner and under then-captain Steve Smith, who elected to look the other way, executed a premeditated plan to alter the ball’s surface during the third Test in Cape Town, in order to promote reverse swing.

Once he was caught, the public outrage and revulsion were overwhelming. Cricket Australia, the national cricket governing body, rushed through an inadequate investigation, omitting many of the touring party, and concluding that knowledge of the plan was confined to Bancroft, Warner and Smith. It imposed draconian penalties: yearlong bans for Smith and Warner, nine months for Bancroft.

Coach Darren Lehmann eventually stood down, followed out the door by several support staff, administrators and board members.

The cone of silence surrounding the affair cracked open with the release of Usman Khawaja’s autobiography, Sabr, in which he alleged everyone in the dressing room was in on the plan. Players and coaching staff came out publicly to either back Khawaja’s story or reject his version of events.

Current team captain Pat Cummins, who was also part of the team in 2018, publicly insisted that he did not know about the use of sandpaper. This was reportedly the final straw for Bancroft: “It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone,” he wrote.

For eight years he had borne the brunt of being labelled a cheat and watched his former teammates carry on with their Test careers – including Smith and Warner, after serving their bans.

Within hours of Cricket Australia’s announcement of an independent “truth forum” that would provide a “safe place” for discussion – a belated effort to stem the tide of damaging public confessions – Bancroft’s self-penned expose was published in The West Australian newspaper.

Not only did he insist that everyone was in on the scheme, but it was not an isolated occurrence, as the investigation had concluded; he had also used sandpaper in the second Test in Gqeberha that year.

“I made a terrible decision because I wanted to belong in the Australian team,” Bancroft wrote.

The context of his choice shouldn’t be overlooked. He was a 24-year-old adult, yet a junior member of the side playing in his seventh Test, and he desperately wanted to fit in.

The years leading up to the South Africa tour were defined by an increasingly toxic culture in which the boundaries of sportsmanship were tested, stretched and treated as pliable when convenient.

The Australian men’s team were the self-appointed guardians of “the line”, their own behaviour consistently justified as being on the right side of what was acceptable under the mantra of playing “hard but fair”. There was a lack of strong and ethical leadership in the dressing room, from the coaching staff all the way up to the Cricket Australia boardroom.

An independent, wide-ranging review by ethics nonprofit organisation The Ethics Centre, conducted in the aftermath of the affair, exposed a culture of “winning without counting the costs” that seeped throughout Cricket Australia. It was a culture in which staff and players feared the consequences of speaking honestly. It is no wonder that silence and dishonesty flourished in order to protect the brand and ensure self-preservation.

“We were frightened,” Bancroft wrote. “We were under pressure. We were trying to manage a situation that was rapidly getting away from us.”

While the on-field reputation of the Australian Test team has improved since 2018, fronted by captains Tim Paine and then Cummins, the blackened seeds sown were nourished by years of resentment and grievance, and have now emerged fully grown in blighted and twisted ugliness.

The complexity and nuance of ball-tampering have been overtaken by accusations of who knew what and a tug-of-war over who owns the truth – not to mention an administration that desperately hoped a web of half-truths and omissions would hold.

It has held a confronting mirror to the wider public’s veneration of “mateship”, the close bond of brotherhood that Australians have long held as core to their national identity. The baggy green cap worn by the country’s Test cricketers has been its unofficial symbol. Friendship may be universal, but mateship – that’s unique to Australia. The cap looks increasingly frayed with every public disclosure.

For Australians to accept that a young player would consider cheating, and then lie about cheating, as the best way of fitting in with his “mates”, it would mean questioning this idea of national exceptionalism. It would mean accepting that self-interest would trump the sacrosanct bonds of selfless “mateship”.

There have been widespread calls for Australian cricket to move on and a growing collective weariness that this unseemly and unflattering saga continues to dominate the news landscape. Perhaps the reflection in the mirror is simply too confronting to sustain the gaze.

There is an alternate universe in which Cricket Australia, in the aftermath of Newlands, could have stood the three central players down for the final Test, pending a full and thorough investigation that would have included all members of the touring party, rather than a select few. The players could have been supported and could have had the moral fortitude to be completely honest. An open and mature public conversation could have taken place about the nature of ball-tampering and any disciplinary action better reflected the nature of the “crime”. Responsibility could have been shared and Cricket Australia could have accepted its full portion.

It wouldn’t have been easy; it would still have been controversial, but it would likely not have been what is now: an omnishambles of human and reputational wreckage that may yet prematurely end careers.

In 2018, Bancroft thought the Australian team “were down the rabbit hole so far”.

Eight years later, Australian cricket has yet to reckon with its own shortcomings, still stuck in a hole of its own making.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: 'Even if they ask me to play as a bowler, I will': Dhruv Jurel's selfless Team India message after crucial 78 vs NZ
articles.summary: Dhruv Jurel underlined his team-first mentality after playing a crucial role in India's batting domination against New Zealand in the first Test at the
articles.body: Dhruv Jurel underlined his team-first mentality after playing a crucial role in India's batting domination against New Zealand in the first Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Sunday. The wicketkeeper-batter, who scored an attacking 78 off 79 deliveries on Day 4, said representing the country was his biggest priority and he would be willing to take up any responsibility for the team.Speaking at the post-day press conference, Jurel highlighted his willingness to contribute in whatever capacity the team requires."For the country, I am ready to play. Even if you ask me to play as a bowler, I will do it," Jurel said, reflecting his commitment to putting the team's interests ahead of individual preferences.'I keep picking his brain': Jurel on Rishabh PantJurel also spoke warmly about his admiration for Rishabh Pant, who produced a sensational 128-run knock to put India in a commanding position. The duo added 75 runs for the sixth wicket in just 60 deliveries, accelerating India's scoring rate before the declaration.Jurel described Pant as a phenomenal player and revealed that he regularly interacts with the left-hander to understand his approach and mindset."I have spoken about him lots of times. He is a phenomenal player. I am always curious about his mindset and keep picking his brain. I love him as a player and as a mentor," Jurel said.Jurel reveals India's declaration strategyThe 25-year-old also explained the thinking behind India's declaration at 720/9. He revealed that the team wanted to maximise its batting time after lunch while ensuring enough overs remained to bowl New Zealand out."We were thinking about giving ourselves 135-140 overs. That was the plan, to bat one hour after lunch and get as many runs as possible," he explained.India eventually declared with a massive 352-run first-innings lead after batting for 166 overs. Jurel's contribution came at a crucial stage, with his 78 off 79 balls featuring seven fours and a six.Earlier, KL Rahul had scored 136, while Yashasvi Jaiswal (85), Devdutt Padikkal (80) and Shubman Gill (98) also made significant contributions. Pant's century provided the finishing flourish to India's innings.India then made early inroads into New Zealand's second innings, with Jasprit Bumrah dismissing Tom Latham for a duck before Prasidh Krishna removed first-innings centurion Henry Nicholls, with Jurel taking a sharp catch at short leg.New Zealand ended Day 4 at 119/2, trailing India by 233 runs, with Devon Conway unbeaten on 59 and Rachin Ravindra on 27.India will head into the final day needing eight more wickets to secure victory and take a 1-0 lead in the series.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: A six to reach 100! Rishabh Pant reveals the habit that has also cost him centuries
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Rishabh Pant wants to bring more consistency to his game and make an impact whenever he steps onto the field.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Rishabh Pant wants to bring more consistency to his game and make an impact whenever he steps onto the field. The India wicketkeeper, who recently became the first Indian wicketkeeper to score Test centuries in all four SENA countries, said being on the field and enjoying the game remain his biggest priorities.Pant answered questions about his fitness and form in style on Sunday, scoring a brilliant 128 off 153 balls in the first Test against New Zealand in Wellington.There had been doubts over his match fitness after a side strain prevented him from playing in the India A matches in New Zealand ahead of the two-Test series. While most of the Test players got valuable match practice, Pant missed out.However, he put those concerns to rest with his impressive hundred. He also became only the sixth Indian batter to score Test centuries in all four SENA countries (South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia).'I just want to be more consistent'Pant has often been known for his attacking batting and ability to hit sixes. However, the wicketkeeper said his focus has now shifted towards consistency and making a difference for the team."See, as a kid, I definitely used to have those goals for sure, hitting a lot of sixes. But you know, right now in my career, I'm not thinking about that anymore."I just want to be more consistent and just make an impact wherever I play the game," Pant told the host broadcaster when asked about surpassing Brendon McCullum to become second on the list of most sixes in Test cricket.'Being on the ground makes me happy'Pant was in his usual cheerful mood behind the stumps after scoring his century. He said he enjoys every moment on the field, whether he is batting or fielding."One thing about me is whenever I take the field, be it fielding or batting, I want to have lots of fun, especially, you know, just being on the ground makes me happy. And just enjoying every day being out on the field," said Pant, who is not part of India's white-ball set-up.With India posting a record 720/9, Pant felt the conditions were good for batting. However, he said Test cricket also requires players to be patient and work hard at the crease."But at the same time you have to enjoy that grind being on the field because every day you won't get a spicy wicket. You have to grind through, especially in Test cricket."So definitely being on the ground, the one thing we enjoy as a team is keep on talking about something, enjoying the little moments and having fun and putting our best effort on the field every day," said Pant.He also added that India would back themselves to take the remaining eight New Zealand wickets on the fifth day.'I was eyeing that hundred for sure'Scoring his first Test century in New Zealand was a special moment for Pant. He said he was determined to stay at the crease for as long as possible and make the most of the opportunity."I think definitely it was a good one. New Zealand was one place where I was eyeing that hundred for sure. And I made sure that in a wicket like this where you have to grind and everyone is batting well, I just wanted to stay there as long as possible and just make my impact," said Pant, who reached his century with a six.The wicketkeeper also revealed that he usually likes to complete his hundreds with a six, but that approach has cost him several centuries in the past."See, mostly whenever I'm trying to get a hundred, I try to get it with a six. But because of that, I've also missed a lot of hundreds. So I was waiting, I was very patient about it. But when the mid-off came up, I was like, this is the right opportunity. I might take it," he added.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'We are pretty behind the game': Rachin Ravindra's frank admission after India's batting blitz leaves New Zealand struggling
articles.summary: New Zealand are staring at a daunting challenge heading into the final day of the first Test against India after being pushed onto the back foot by a
articles.body: New Zealand are staring at a daunting challenge heading into the final day of the first Test against India after being pushed onto the back foot by a record-breaking batting performance from the visitors. With India declaring at 720/9 to secure a massive 352-run first-innings lead, the hosts have little room for error as they look to survive the final 90 overs.Acknowledging the difficult position, New Zealand batter Rachin Ravindra admitted that his side were well behind in the contest and would need to show resilience with the bat on the final day."We are pretty behind the game. India batted well. It's about batting as long as possible for us," Ravindra said after stumps on Day 4.New Zealand ended the day at 119/2 in their second innings, still trailing India by 233 runs. Devon Conway was unbeaten on 59, while Ravindra was batting on 27, with the pair tasked with leading the resistance on the final day.'Take it ball by ball': Ravindra on New Zealand's survival challengeWith 90 overs scheduled on the final day, Ravindra said New Zealand would avoid looking too far ahead and instead concentrate on tackling the challenge one delivery at a time."Saving the game is looking quite far ahead, so we would take it ball by ball. It's 90 overs on the final day," he said.'I am Dev's biggest supporter': Ravindra backs ConwayRavindra also threw his weight behind opening partner Devon Conway, backing the experienced batter to convert starts into substantial scores if he spends enough time at the crease."I am Dev's biggest supporter. Whenever he bats a good number of balls, he scores," Ravindra said.However, Ravindra refused to view the batting-friendly conditions as a negative for Test cricket, pointing out that the contest had produced plenty of entertainment."Don't think it is a negative thing to see Glenn Phillips, Nicholls, Rahul, Pant score hundreds. It might not be a typical Welly wicket where we stand 30 yards from the wicket, but anything is a good advert for Test cricket," he said.More than 1,000 runs have already been scored across the first two innings, with 1,088 runs highlighting the assistance the surface has offered to batters.'Bumrah is always pretty switched on': Ravindra on India's pace spearheadRavindra also acknowledged the intensity of India's pace attack, particularly Jasprit Bumrah, whose relentless approach continued to put pressure on the New Zealand batters. Asked about Bumrah's intensity, especially during his final over of the day, the New Zealand all-rounder said such commitment was part of the demands of Test cricket."Bumrah is always pretty switched on. That's Test cricket," he said.On whether the surface could offer greater assistance to spinners on the final day, Ravindra suggested that weather conditions, particularly wind, could influence how the pitch behaves."I don't have a crystal ball gaze, but if it's a bit more windy, it might get drier and might turn. Let's see," he added.With New Zealand still 233 runs behind and eight wickets in hand, the final day promises a stern examination of their batting resolve as India look to wrap up the contest and take a 1-0 lead in the series.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: IND vs NZ: New Zealand look to Martin Crowe, Brendon McCullum for inspiration as they fight to save Test
articles.summary: New Zealand face a huge challenge to save the first Test against India after conceding a 352-run first-innings lead at the Basin Reserve in Wellington.
articles.body: New Zealand face a huge challenge to save the first Test against India after conceding a 352-run first-innings lead at the Basin Reserve in Wellington. With eight wickets in hand and a minimum of 90 overs left on the final day, the hosts will need a remarkable batting effort to deny India victory.Devon Conway and Rachin Ravindra will have to lead the fightback on Monday. The two left-handers were unbeaten at the close of play on Day 4, with Conway scoring 59 and Ravindra making 27. Their partnership was worth 59 runs as New Zealand reached 119/2 at stumps, still trailing by 233 runs.The task is difficult, but New Zealand can draw inspiration from two famous batting performances at the same venue by Martin Crowe and Brendon McCullum.Crowe, McCullum set the benchmarkNew Zealand have twice produced remarkable batting performances at this venue to save a Test match.The longest they have batted in the third or fourth innings of a Test to save a match was 220.3 overs against Sri Lanka in 1991. They scored 671/4 in that innings. Their second-longest effort came against India in 2014, when they batted for 210 overs and scored 680/8 declared.Both innings featured two of the greatest individual batting performances in New Zealand's Test history. Crowe scored a magnificent 299 against Sri Lanka in 1991, while McCullum made 302 against India in 2014.Conway and Ravindra will need something special of their own if New Zealand are to survive the final day.Conway leads New Zealand's fightbackConway gave New Zealand some hope with an unbeaten half-century before stumps. He was joined by Ravindra as the hosts tried to recover from India's massive first-innings total of 720/9.India's total was the highest ever by a team in a Test innings in New Zealand. It also put the visitors in a commanding position after the hosts had managed 368 in their first innings.New Zealand still need another 233 runs just to make India bat again, while the visitors have eight wickets to take to seal the match.Pant's century powers India to record totalIndia's massive total was built on outstanding contributions from their top-order batters.KL Rahul led the way with 136. He added 130 runs for the opening wicket with Yashasvi Jaiswal, who scored 85. Rahul then shared a 165-run stand with Devdutt Padikkal (80) and added another 91 with captain Shubman Gill, who scored 98 before getting out two balls before the end of the third day.Rishabh Pant then took charge with an attacking 128 off 153 balls. He added 100 runs with Gill, 68 with nightwatchman Anshul Kamboj and 75 with Dhruv Jurel, who scored 78.Pant's century was the ninth of his Test career and his fourth since returning to the format in 2024, two years after his serious car accident.Pant said scoring a century in New Zealand was special, as it was a place where he had been keen to reach the milestone.“I think definitely it was a good innings. New Zealand was one place where I was eyeing that century for sure,” Pant said. “In a match like this where everyone has to grind and is batting well I just wanted to stay there as long as possible and make my impact.“I just keep it simple most of the time. Whenever I see the ball I try to hit it.”Pant enjoyed taking on the New Zealand bowlers and fielders, who had five players stationed near the boundary. He used a wide range of shots, including three sixes down the ground, shots behind square and several boundaries on the leg side. He also played his trademark reverse sweep.With Pant and Jurel scoring quickly, India were able to declare their innings midway through the second session. Jurel completed his third Test half-century off 61 balls.Bumrah strikes twice, Nicholls falls againJasprit Bumrah gave India an early breakthrough in New Zealand's second innings by dismissing captain Tom Latham for a duck.Bumrah had also dismissed Latham in the first innings, bowling him with the third ball of New Zealand's innings after beating him with a delivery that moved back in from outside off stump.This time, the India pacer produced a delivery that moved away after pitching. Latham pushed forward tentatively and edged the ball to wicketkeeper Pant.Henry Nicholls, who had scored an unbeaten 175 in the first innings, began New Zealand's second innings with the third ball. He looked comfortable while making 31 but was eventually dismissed by Prasidh Krishna.Nicholls edged Krishna's delivery onto his thigh pad, and the ball popped up for Jurel to take an athletic catch on the leg side.Bumrah returned to bowl the final over of the day with seven fielders on the leg side, but India could not pick up another wicket.With Conway and Ravindra at the crease, New Zealand will need a long and determined effort on the final day to keep the match alive.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: England: Will Jacks out of T20 Australia tour with broken hand
articles.summary: England all-rounder Will Jacks is ruled out of the rest of the tour of Australia with a broken hand.
articles.body:
England all-rounder Will Jacks has been ruled out of the rest of the tour of Australia with a broken hand.

The 28-year-old was injured after four balls of the penultimate over as Australia took victory in the first T20 international in Melbourne on Saturday.

Jacks was hurt trying to take a caught-and-bowled chance off Ben Dwarshuis.

The injury means versatile Tom Banton will skipper the side for the fifth and final T20 in Canberra on 2 December.

Jacks had been pencilled in for the job as regular captain Harry Brook will leave Australia early to prepare for the tour of South Africa.

England begin the first of three Tests against South Africa on 17 December.
